A Softer Grip

Costume designer Imani Cole builds garments that must bend, stretch, and hold their shape through repeated performances. She studies folds and flexible seams, to control[1] how fabric moves around a body. A university robotics laboratory invited Cole to examine a different movement problem: a mechanical gripper could lift firm boxes but often dropped soft or irregular objects. Cole's knowledge of layered fabric imitated[2] a possible solution because padding can distribute pressure without eliminating flexibility.

At the laboratory, Cole watched two rigid gripping fingers close around a foam model of a pear. The fingers pinched its narrow center, tilted the model, and dropping[3] it onto the table. For example,[4] Cole noticed that the contact occurred at only two small points. A hand, by contrast, can wrap several surfaces around an object. The observation suggested that the gripper needed a covering able to change shape as it closed.

Cole stitched a sleeve from alternating panels of mesh and padded cloth. The first prototype looked like the most insanely fantastic robot glove ever made[5]. Cole preferred silver thread, although the laboratory also stocked black and blue thread.[6] Narrow channels allowed the sleeve to fold in predictable places, while the padding compressed against uneven surfaces. Engineers attached the sleeve to the existing fingers rather than rebuilding the gripper itself.

During a test, the covered fingers approached a plastic cup lying on its side. The mesh relaxed as the fingers opened. Then the sleeve creased around the cup's rim, flattened against its curved wall, and held the cup level as the gripper lifted.[7] Unlike the earlier rigid contact at two points.[8] Pressure sensors showed that the covered gripper spread force across a wider area.

[A] The team tested several versions of the sleeve. [B] Each revision altered one feature, such as padding thickness or channel spacing. [C] The final design improved three tasks; lifting the cup, holding the foam pear, and carrying a fabric pouch[9]. [D] The collaboration succeeded not because costume design and robotics became identical, but because a principle from one field could be tested carefully in another.[10]
